editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: Japan’s cartridge-console contest begins in earnest, while home-computer players trade resources, paint by touch and command robots through a crisis.
morningLine: Friday, July 15, brings Nintendo’s red-and-white Family Computer to Japanese shops with three familiar arcade names ready to play at home.

milestone.title: Nintendo launches the Family Computer
milestone.note: The July 15 Japanese debut created the hardware and software platform later exported as the NES, helping define the modern console business.

lead.headline: Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home With Its Family Computer
lead.dek: At ¥14,800, Nintendo’s red-and-white Famicom arrives with two controllers and three arcade conversions.
body: Nintendo launched its Family Computer in Japan on July 15, placing a compact red-and-white cartridge machine on shop counters for ¥14,800. The name was quickly shortened to Famicom, and the proposition was direct: swap a cartridge and bring the speed and familiarity of the arcade into the living room.

The console arrived with two hard-wired controllers. Its second pad carried an unusual microphone, while the initial software lineup leaned entirely on proven coin-operated hits: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr. and Popeye. Nintendo’s own history stresses cartridge changing and arcade-style play as the machine’s essential appeal.

That opening trio made the launch easy to understand. Rather than asking families to imagine what a new platform might someday do, Nintendo put recognizable characters and play patterns at the front of the counter from day one.

The week also finds Sega introducing its SG-1000 at nearly the same price, making Japan a testing ground for rival visions of the cartridge home console. The Family Computer would later be redesigned for overseas sale as the Nintendo Entertainment System; together, the Famicom and NES ultimately sold more than 60 million units.

stories.headline: Sega Enters the Living Room With the SG-1000
stories.dek: Sega’s first home cartridge system challenges Nintendo at roughly the same price.
body: Sega entered Japan’s home-console market in July with the SG-1000, a ¥15,000 cartridge system closely related to the company’s SC-3000 computer hardware. Its arrival put Sega within ¥200 of Nintendo’s new Famicom.

Early software included N-Sub, Mahjong, Congo Bongo, Yamato, Star Jacker and shogi. Historical accounts commonly associate the machine with July 15, though the surviving evidence makes the exact day less certain than the month; what is clear is that Sega and Nintendo began competing for the same living-room shelf in the summer of 1983.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. Turns Economics Into a Multiplayer Contest
stories.dek: Dani Bunten makes supply, demand and bargaining the center of play.
body: Electronic Arts’ M.U.L.E., featured in the July-August Computer Gaming World, sends as many as four colonists to develop land and outfit mechanical M.U.L.E. workers for production. Food, energy, smithore and crystite become the raw materials of both survival and rivalry.

Its auctions turn economics into a social contest. Shortages, bargaining, collusion and sudden swings in supply are visible around the screen, giving Atari computer owners a multiplayer game in which reading the room can matter as much as reading the numbers.

stories.headline: Infocom's Suspended Puts Six Robots Between the Player and Disaster
stories.dek: A frozen overseer must save a planet through six very different mechanical senses.
body: Infocom’s Suspended: The Cryogenic Nightmare places the player immobilized inside a life-support complex while planetary systems fail. Commands must pass through six robots, each able to perceive and act on the emergency in a different way.

Michael Berlyn’s design turns limited information into the puzzle: the player must combine incomplete reports, dispatch the right machine and repair the system before disaster spreads. Its raised plastic face and elaborate documents also continue Infocom’s habit of making the package part of the fiction.
